newsitem.title: USA: Launch of U.S. shuttle is pushed back to Saturday.
newsitem.headline: Launch of U.S. shuttle is pushed back to Saturday.

text.p: NASA postponed the blastoff of the Columbia space shuttle to Saturday from Friday to make way for the launch of an unmanned rocket, officials said.
They said the space agency had been forced to push the date back so an Atlas rocket, grounded on Wednesday by gusty winds, could be launched on Thursday.
The space vehicles use the same U.S. Air Force tracking facilities at Cape Canaveral, and it takes about 48 hours to reprogram the equipment for a different launch.
The commercial Atlas, carrying a European television satellite, had booked its slot before the shuttle and therefore had priority over the National Aeronautics and Space Agency flight.

But if bad weather scrubs the Atlas' Thursday launch, it would have to line up for the first available future slot. If the Columbia cannot lift off on Saturday, it would still have one postponement date left.
NASA spokesman George Diller said Columbia's countdown would be put on hold for 24 hours to reset blastoff for 2:51 p.m. (1951 GMT) on Saturday,
The shuttle was already running one week late because of booster-rocket problems.
Meteorologists gave Columbia just a 1-in-5 chance of getting off the launch pad on Saturday, mainly because of high winds. Conditions were not expected to improve on Sunday.
"I really don't see a lot of options until we get well into next week," shuttle weather officer Ed Priselac said. "Unfortunately, things don't look very good."

Columbia is due to spend 16 days in orbit while its crew of five astronauts conducts scientific research with a pair of free-flying satellites. Two spacewalks are also planned, as practice for building an international space station.
